issues.description: In Experiment 1, 17 out of 40 participants (42.5%) were excluded because they had fewer than 10 high-confidence trials in a cell. This massive attrition rate introduces a significant selection bias, as the final sample only represents individuals who are highly confident in their memory, potentially skewing the results toward those most susceptible to the 'illusion' construct.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (17 participants were excluded)

issues.description: The authors report a Bayes Factor (BFincl) of 2.45 for the three-way interaction in Experiment 1. According to standard Bayesian interpretation (and the authors' own stated criteria), this is 'anecdotal evidence.' However, they proceed to discuss the 12% increase in illusory errors as a meaningful finding supporting their hypothesis.
issues.quote: Finally, there is only anecdotal evidence for a three-way interaction between Target Type, Error Type and Memory Delay (BFincl = 2.45): For pseudo-letter targets, illusory errors increase 12% as memory deteriorates

issues.description: In the 'Short with Interference' condition of Experiment 1, the second letter display (interference) appears simultaneously with the cue. This design choice makes it impossible to distinguish between memory interference and attentional disruption during the retrieval/cued-selection phase.
issues.quote: The Short with Interference condition (panel B) was the same as the Short condition, except that now the second letter display appeared together with the cue.

issues.description: The study relies on 'high confidence' to distinguish 'illusions' from 'guesses.' However, confidence is a subjective metacognitive measure and does not inherently prove that a memory trace was 'reshaped.' High confidence errors can also arise from misperception at encoding or biased retrieval strategies that the participant is unaware of.
issues.quote: Focusing on memory illusions instead of general false memory reports allows a separation of such incorrect but seemingly true memories from memory lapses that are filled in by best guesses

issues.description: Across all four experiments, the authors report Bayes Factors but fail to provide standard effect size estimates (e.g., Cohen's d, partial eta-squared). This makes it difficult to assess the practical significance or magnitude of the observed shifts in error rates.
issues.quote: The Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA showed that a model with main effects for Error Type, Target Type, and Memory Delay... had the best fit (BFm = 18)

issues.description: Experiments 3 and 4 used a sequential analysis stopping rule (BF > 10). While Bayesian stopping rules are more robust than frequentist ones, the authors do not specify the prior distribution used for these sequential checks, nor do they report the BF values at each 'look,' which is necessary for transparency in sequential designs.
issues.quote: Note that in this experiment the number of participants was determined based on a stopping rule implemented in an ongoing sequential analysis of the Bayes Factor for the critical t-test... once the outcome crossed a BF of 10, testing would stop.

issues.description: The increase in errors over time is attributed to 'memory reshaping.' However, it could also be explained by retrieval-based interference: as the memory trace weakens, the presence of the 'real' letter in the response display acts as a more powerful distractor/competitor, leading to a selection bias at the moment of the test rather than a change in the stored trace.
issues.quote: This increase in errors over time indicates that the high confidence errors do not (purely) result from incorrect perceptual encoding of the memory display.

issues.description: Experiment 1 included a 'none of these' option, whereas Experiment 2 removed it. This change in the response set size and the forced-choice nature of Experiment 2-4 changes the task's cognitive demands and the baseline probability of errors, making direct comparisons across experiments problematic.
issues.quote: Since the target letter (and its counterpart) were always among the response options, the response option 'none of these' was eliminated.

issues.description: The study only uses Latin alphabet letters. The 'world knowledge' effect claimed may be specific to highly overlearned symbolic categories and may not generalize to other forms of short-term memory (e.g., spatial, color, or novel object memory).
issues.quote: In this case, the relevant expectations relate to a highly overlearned category of visual symbols, namely letters of the alphabet.

issues.description: The training task in Experiment 1 used rectangles/orientations, but the main task used letters. It is unclear if the 75% accuracy threshold on rectangles is a valid predictor of 'minimal proficiency' for a letter-based memory illusion task.
issues.quote: In this training task, participants were instructed to indicate whether the rectangle at a cued location in a memory display had the same orientation as the rectangle at that same location in a test display.

issues.description: The authors state they used JASP for Bayesian ANOVAs but do not specify the prior distributions (e.g., Cauchy scale). Since Bayes Factors can be sensitive to the choice of priors, this is a gap in reporting necessary for replication.
issues.quote: The resulting data were analysed in a Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA in JASP 0.16.4

issues.description: The authors invoke 'predictive processing' as a framework, but they do not provide a formal model or specific parameters (e.g., precision-weighting) that would distinguish their findings from simpler models of proactive interference or decay-based retrieval bias.
issues.quote: Our findings support a predictive processing view of the formation and maintenance of memory

issues.description: In Experiment 2, the exclusion rate for participants was 31.7%. The 'included' group had a high-confidence rate of 49.2%, while the 'excluded' group had only 15.7%. This suggests the results only apply to a specific sub-population with high metacognitive confidence, limiting the study's generalizability.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials... resulted in an inclusion of 198 participants (92 participants were excluded)

issues.description: Experiment 4 was conducted online via Zoom. There is no reporting on how the authors controlled for screen size, viewing distance, or environmental distractions, which are critical for a task involving brief (250ms) visual presentations and mirrored letters.
issues.quote: Second the data was collected in an online experiment, using Neurotask scripting... participants were given the link to the Neurotask experiment, which they then started on their own laptop.

issues.description: In Table 1, the BFincl for 'Target Type' and 'Error Type' are reported as 1.462e+14. While possible in very large effects, such extreme values in a sample of N=23 suggest potential issues with model convergence or data entry errors in the JASP output.
issues.quote: BFincl | 1.462e+14

issues.description: In Experiment 4, the authors state that a BF of 0.45 is 'anecdotal evidence against' the three-way interaction, yet in Experiment 1, a BF of 2.45 (similarly anecdotal) is used to support the hypothesis. This indicates an inconsistent threshold for evidence across experiments.
issues.quote: with a Bfincl = 0.45 showing anecdotal evidence against including the three-way interaction

issues.description: The exclusion of symmetrical letters (A, H, I, etc.) is necessary for the design but significantly restricts the stimulus space. This might make the 'pseudo-letter' category more salient or predictable than it would be in a naturalistic setting.
issues.quote: Therefore only letters that changed when mirrored were included in the experiment (i.e. the symmetrical letters A,H,I,M,O,T,U,V,W,X,Y were excluded)

issues.description: The authors argue against the 'weaker memory trace' explanation by saying pseudo-letters should lead to random guessing. However, a weaker trace for pseudo-letters combined with a constant response bias toward real letters would produce the exact same 'increase over time' pattern without requiring a 'reshaping' of the memory trace itself.
issues.quote: If that were the case, participants remembering a pseudo-letter target... should be selecting all items in the probe display with equal probability

issues.description: The age range in Experiment 2 (18-56) is much broader than in Experiment 1 (19-30). The authors do not analyze whether age (and thus length of exposure to the alphabet) correlates with the strength of the 'illusion,' which would be a key test of their 'world knowledge' hypothesis.
issues.quote: 290 participants took part (164 female; age range 18-56 years, average age 20.3 years)

issues.description: In Experiment 3, one participant was excluded from the ANOVA due to listwise deletion. While N=1 is small, the use of listwise deletion in a design already suffering from high attrition further biases the sample toward 'perfect' responders.
issues.quote: Because of listwise deletion of missing values (resulting from 0 high confidence responses in one or more of the cells of the design), one participant was excluded from the main ANOVA.
